note: Core school-science ideas the assistant can explain without an experiment on the bench. Each entry: a full explanation (text), a one-line everyday version (simple), optional display LaTeX and a page to open. Drafted for LABscape; have a subject teacher review before release.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that still behaves like that element. It has a tiny, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons arranged in shells around it. Atoms are electrically neutral because the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
entries.simple: An atom is the tiny building block that everything is made of.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Protons (charge +1) and neutrons (no charge) sit in the nucleus and carry almost all of an atom's mass. Electrons (charge -1) are about 1/1836 of a proton's mass and occupy shells around the nucleus. The number of protons is the atomic number and decides which element the atom is.
entries.simple: Protons and neutrons sit in the middle of an atom; much lighter electrons move around them.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom, so every atom has the same number of protons. Elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical reactions. They are arranged in the periodic table in order of atomic number.
entries.simple: An element is a pure substance made of just one kind of atom, like oxygen or gold.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: A compound is a substance in which atoms of two or more elements are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio, such as water (H2O) or sodium chloride (NaCl). Its properties differ from those of the elements in it, and it can only be separated into elements by a chemical reaction.
entries.simple: A compound is made when different kinds of atoms join together, like hydrogen and oxygen making water.

entries.subject: chemistry
aliases: difference between a mixture and a compound
entries.text: A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically bonded, so each keeps its own properties and the proportions can vary. Mixtures can be separated by physical methods such as filtration, evaporation, distillation or chromatography.
entries.simple: A mixture is substances jumbled together without joining, like sand in water, so you can separate them again.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: A molecule is a group of two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds. It can be an element (O2) or a compound (CO2). The molecular formula tells you how many atoms of each element one molecule contains.
entries.simple: A molecule is a few atoms stuck together to act as one particle.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: An ion is an atom or group of atoms with an electric charge because it has lost or gained electrons. Metals usually lose electrons to form positive ions (cations); non-metals usually gain electrons to form negative ions (anions).
entries.simple: An ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons, so it carries a charge.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they have different mass numbers. They react chemically in the same way; some, such as carbon-14, are radioactive.
entries.simple: Isotopes are versions of the same element whose atoms have different numbers of neutrons.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: The mole is the chemist's counting unit for particles. One mole contains 6.022 x 10^23 particles (the Avogadro constant), and one mole of a substance has a mass in grams equal to its relative formula mass. So 18 g of water is one mole of water molecules. Amount in moles = mass / molar mass.
entries.simple: A mole is just a very big number of particles, the way a dozen means twelve, so chemists can count atoms by weighing them.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol. Numerically it equals the relative formula mass: add up the relative atomic masses of every atom in the formula. For CO2 that is 12 + 16 + 16 = 44 g/mol.
entries.simple: Molar mass is how many grams one mole of a substance weighs.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Concentration tells you how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution, usually in mol/dm3 (mol/L) or g/dm3. Concentration = amount of solute / volume of solution. Diluting a solution lowers its concentration but does not change the amount of solute.
entries.simple: Concentration is how much stuff is dissolved in a certain amount of liquid: strong squash is more concentrated than weak squash.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: A solution is a mixture in which a solute is spread evenly through a solvent so that it cannot be seen. In salt water, salt is the solute and water the solvent. Dissolving is a physical change: the solute can be recovered by evaporating the solvent.
entries.simple: When something dissolves it spreads out through the liquid so finely you cannot see it; the result is a solution.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Solubility is the maximum mass of a solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature. A saturated solution holds that maximum. For most solids solubility rises with temperature, which is why crystals form when a hot saturated solution cools.
entries.simple: Solubility is how much of something will dissolve; once no more will dissolve, the solution is saturated.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: An acid is a substance that releases hydrogen ions (H+) in water, giving a pH below 7. Acids turn blue litmus red, react with bases to form a salt and water, with carbonates to release carbon dioxide, and with reactive metals to release hydrogen. Strong acids ionise completely; weak acids only partly.
entries.simple: An acid is a sour, sometimes corrosive substance, like the acid in lemon juice or vinegar, with a pH below 7.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: A base neutralises an acid to form a salt and water. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, releasing hydroxide ions (OH-) and giving a pH above 7. Alkalis turn red litmus blue and feel soapy.
entries.simple: A base is the chemical opposite of an acid; one that dissolves in water is called an alkali.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: pH measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is. It runs from about 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline. pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, so each step of 1 means a tenfold change in acidity.
entries.simple: pH is a number that says how acidic or alkaline something is: 7 is neutral, lower is acidic, higher is alkaline.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: An indicator is a dye that changes colour with pH. Litmus is red in acid and blue in alkali; phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in alkali; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali; universal indicator shows a range of colours across the pH scale.
entries.simple: An indicator is a dye that changes colour to show whether something is an acid or an alkali.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base to form a salt and water. In solution the essential change is hydrogen ions joining hydroxide ions to make water. The reaction releases heat.
entries.simple: Neutralisation is an acid and an alkali cancelling each other out to make a salt and water.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: In chemistry a salt is an ionic compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion. Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, sulfuric acid gives sulfates and nitric acid gives nitrates. Table salt, sodium chloride, is one example.
entries.simple: A salt is what you get, along with water, when an acid reacts with a base; table salt is just one kind.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: A titration finds the concentration of a solution by reacting a measured volume of it with a solution of known concentration, added from a burette until an indicator shows the end point. The volume added, the titre, is used with the balanced equation to calculate the unknown concentration.
entries.simple: A titration is carefully adding one solution to another until the reaction is just complete, to work out how strong one of them is.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: A precipitate is an insoluble solid that forms when two solutions react. It makes the mixture cloudy and can be filtered off. For example, silver nitrate and sodium chloride solutions give a white precipitate of silver chloride.
entries.simple: A precipitate is a solid that suddenly appears when two clear liquids are mixed, making them cloudy.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Oxidation is the loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen); reduction is the gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen). The two always happen together in a redox reaction. An oxidising agent takes electrons and is itself reduced; a reducing agent gives electrons and is itself oxidised.
entries.simple: Oxidation is losing electrons and reduction is gaining them, and one never happens without the other (OIL RIG).

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up. It provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful. Enzymes are biological catalysts made of protein.
entries.simple: A catalyst is a helper that makes a reaction go faster without being used up itself.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature rises: combustion and neutralisation are examples. An endothermic reaction takes energy in, so the temperature falls: dissolving ammonium nitrate and thermal decomposition are examples.
entries.simple: Exothermic reactions give out heat and feel warm; endothermic ones take heat in and feel cold.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: The rate of reaction is how fast reactants turn into products. Particles must collide with at least the activation energy to react. Raising the temperature or concentration, increasing surface area or adding a catalyst gives more successful collisions each second, so the rate rises.
entries.simple: Reactions go faster when the particles bump into each other more often and harder: heat, stirring, finer powder or a catalyst all help.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: In a physical change, such as melting or dissolving, no new substance is made and the change is usually easy to reverse. In a chemical change new substances form: signs include a colour change, a gas, a precipitate or an energy change, and it is usually hard to reverse.
entries.simple: A physical change only alters how something looks; a chemical change makes a brand new substance.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: In a chemical reaction atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed, so the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants. If the mass seems to change, a gas has usually entered or left the container.
entries.simple: Nothing is lost in a reaction: the same atoms are there before and after, just joined differently.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. Write the correct formulae first, then change only the big numbers in front (coefficients), never the small numbers inside a formula. Count each element in turn, leave hydrogen and oxygen until last, and check again at the end.
entries.simple: To balance an equation, put numbers in front of the formulae until each kind of atom appears the same number of times on both sides.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Ionic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. It forms when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal. Ionic compounds form giant lattices with high melting points and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved.
entries.simple: An ionic bond forms when one atom gives electrons to another and the two charged atoms then attract each other.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms. Simple molecules such as water have low melting points because the forces between molecules are weak; giant covalent structures such as diamond have very high melting points.
entries.simple: A covalent bond is two atoms holding on to each other by sharing electrons.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: In a metal, positive ions sit in a regular lattice surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. The attraction between them is the metallic bond. The free electrons carry charge and heat, which is why metals conduct, and layers of ions can slide, which makes metals malleable.
entries.simple: Metal atoms share a sea of loose electrons, which is why metals conduct electricity and can be bent.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: The periodic table lists the elements in order of atomic number. Columns are groups: elements in a group have the same number of outer electrons and so similar chemistry. Rows are periods: elements in a period have the same number of electron shells.
entries.simple: The periodic table is a chart of all the elements, arranged so that similar ones line up in columns.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: The reactivity series ranks metals by how readily they lose electrons: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from a solution of its salt.
entries.simple: The reactivity series is a league table of metals; a more reactive metal can push a less reactive one out of its compound.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Electrolysis uses a direct current to break down an ionic compound that is molten or dissolved (the electrolyte). Positive ions move to the negative electrode (cathode) and gain electrons; negative ions move to the positive electrode (anode) and lose electrons.
entries.simple: Electrolysis is using electricity to split a compound apart.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Combustion is a fast exothermic reaction of a fuel with oxygen. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water; with too little oxygen, incomplete combustion also gives carbon monoxide and soot. A fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat.
entries.simple: Combustion is burning: a fuel reacting with oxygen and giving out heat and light.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: In a solid, particles are packed in fixed positions and only vibrate. In a liquid they stay close but can move past each other, so liquids flow. In a gas they are far apart and move quickly in all directions, so gases fill their container and can be compressed.
entries.simple: Solids keep their shape, liquids flow and gases spread out, because their particles are packed differently.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Melting and boiling happen at fixed temperatures for a pure substance; the energy supplied separates the particles rather than raising the temperature. Evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature, as the fastest particles escape, which is why it cools the liquid left behind.
entries.simple: Heating gives particles enough energy to break free: solids melt, liquids boil, and puddles slowly evaporate.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, caused by their random motion. It is faster in gases than in liquids, and faster at higher temperatures.
entries.simple: Diffusion is particles spreading out on their own, like a smell drifting across a room.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. Evaporation or crystallisation recovers a dissolved solid. Simple distillation recovers the solvent, and fractional distillation separates liquids with different boiling points. Chromatography separates dissolved substances, such as dyes, by how far they travel.
entries.simple: You can separate mixtures by filtering, evaporating, distilling or chromatography, depending on what is mixed.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Hydrocarbons contain only hydrogen and carbon. Alkanes have single bonds only (saturated, general formula CnH2n+2). Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond (unsaturated, CnH2n), which makes them more reactive: they decolourise bromine water, alkanes do not.
entries.simple: Hydrocarbons are fuels made only of hydrogen and carbon; alkenes have a double bond that makes them more reactive than alkanes.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: An ester forms when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, usually with a concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst; water is the other product. Esters have sweet, fruity smells and are used in flavourings and perfumes.
entries.simple: Esters are sweet-smelling compounds made from an acid and an alcohol.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Rusting is the corrosion of iron: iron reacts with oxygen and water to form hydrated iron(III) oxide. Both air and water are needed, and salt speeds it up. It is prevented by painting, oiling, galvanising with zinc or sacrificial protection.
entries.simple: Rust forms when iron reacts with air and water together.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: The limiting reagent is the reactant that is used up first and so decides how much product can form. Any other reactant is in excess. Work it out by comparing the moles of each reactant with the ratio in the balanced equation.
entries.simple: The limiting reagent is the ingredient that runs out first and stops the reaction.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Percentage yield compares the mass of product actually obtained with the maximum predicted from the equation: actual yield / theoretical yield x 100. It is below 100% when the reaction is incomplete, side reactions occur or product is lost on transfer.
entries.simple: Percentage yield is how much product you really got compared with the most you could have got.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and algae use light energy, absorbed by chlorophyll, to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. It is endothermic, and it is the source of the oxygen in the air and of the food at the base of most food chains.
entries.simple: Photosynthesis is how plants use sunlight to make their own food from water and carbon dioxide, giving out oxygen.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.text: Respiration is the exothermic reaction in living cells that releases energy from glucose. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and gives carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen and releases much less energy.
entries.simple: Respiration is how living cells release the energy stored in food.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Speed is the distance travelled per unit time. Velocity is speed in a stated direction, so it is a vector. Average speed = total distance / total time. On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed.
entries.simple: Speed is how fast you are going; velocity is how fast and in which direction.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: change in velocity divided by the time taken, in m/s2. Slowing down is a negative acceleration. On a velocity-time graph the gradient is the acceleration and the area under the line is the distance travelled.
entries.simple: Acceleration is how quickly something speeds up, slows down or changes direction.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's speed, direction or shape. It is a vector measured in newtons (N). If the forces on an object are balanced, the resultant force is zero and its velocity does not change; an unbalanced force makes it accelerate.
entries.simple: A force is a push or a pull.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Newton's first law: an object stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed unless a resultant force acts on it. This resistance to a change in motion is called inertia, and it is greater for a greater mass.
entries.simple: Things keep doing what they are doing, staying still or moving steadily, unless a force changes that.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Newton's second law: the acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force on it and inversely proportional to its mass. Resultant force = mass x acceleration.
entries.simple: The harder you push something, the faster it speeds up; the heavier it is, the slower it speeds up.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Newton's third law: when object A exerts a force on object B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The two forces are the same type and act on different objects, so they do not cancel out.
entries.simple: Every push gets an equal push back: you push the ground backwards and it pushes you forwards.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: First law: an object keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless a resultant force acts. Second law: resultant force = mass x acceleration. Third law: every force has an equal and opposite force acting on the other object.
entries.simple: Newton's three laws say objects keep going unless pushed, bigger pushes mean bigger speed changes, and every push is pushed back.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, in kilograms, and is the same everywhere. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, in newtons: weight = mass x gravitational field strength (about 9.8 N/kg on Earth). On the Moon your mass is unchanged but your weight is about one sixth.
entries.simple: Mass is how much stuff is in you; weight is how hard gravity pulls on it.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Gravity is the attractive force between all masses. Near the Earth's surface it gives every falling object, ignoring air resistance, the same acceleration of about 9.8 m/s2, whatever its mass.
entries.simple: Gravity is the pull that draws things towards each other, and towards the Earth.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact; air resistance (drag) is friction with the air and grows with speed. A falling object reaches terminal velocity when drag equals its weight, so the resultant force is zero.
entries.simple: Friction is the rubbing force that slows things down.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Momentum is mass x velocity, a vector measured in kg m/s. In any collision or explosion with no external force the total momentum before equals the total momentum after. Impulse, force x time, equals the change in momentum.
entries.simple: Momentum is how hard it is to stop a moving thing: more mass or more speed means more momentum.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Energy is the capacity to do work, measured in joules (J). It is held in stores such as kinetic, gravitational potential, chemical, elastic and thermal. Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores; in every transfer some is dissipated as heat.
entries.simple: Energy is what makes things happen, and it is never used up, only moved from one place or form to another.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Kinetic energy is the energy of a moving object, half x mass x speed squared. Gravitational potential energy is the energy an object has because of its height: mass x g x height. As an object falls, potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy.
entries.simple: Kinetic energy is the energy of moving; potential energy is energy stored by being high up.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force: work done = force x distance moved along the force, in joules. Work done equals the energy transferred.
entries.simple: Work is done whenever a force moves something.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred or work is done: power = energy / time, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). In a circuit, power = current x voltage.
entries.simple: Power is how quickly energy is used: a 100 W bulb uses energy twice as fast as a 50 W one.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Pressure is force per unit area, in pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m2). In a fluid, pressure acts in all directions and increases with depth and with the fluid's density.
entries.simple: Pressure is how concentrated a force is: a sharp pin presses harder than a flat thumb with the same push.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Density is mass per unit volume, in kg/m3 or g/cm3. Water has a density of 1 g/cm3. An object floats in a fluid if its average density is lower than the fluid's.
entries.simple: Density is how much mass is packed into a given space: a brick is denser than a sponge of the same size.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: A fluid pushes up on any object in it with a force called upthrust, equal to the weight of the fluid displaced (Archimedes' principle). The object floats when the upthrust can balance its weight, which happens when its average density is less than the fluid's.
entries.simple: Things float when the water they push aside weighs as much as they do.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water. When water freezes, hydrogen bonds hold its molecules in an open hexagonal lattice that takes up about 9% more space than the same molecules in the liquid. Water is unusual: most solids are denser than their liquids. Water is densest at about 4 degrees C.
entries.simple: When water freezes its molecules lock into an open pattern with gaps, so ice is lighter for its size than water and floats.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Temperature measures how hot something is and reflects the average kinetic energy of its particles. Heat is energy transferred from a hotter object to a colder one. A bath of warm water holds more thermal energy than a cup of boiling water, although its temperature is lower.
entries.simple: Temperature is how hot something is; heat is energy moving from a hot thing to a colder one.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree C. Energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change. Water's value is high, 4200 J/kg C, so it heats and cools slowly.
entries.simple: Specific heat capacity is how much energy it takes to warm something up; water needs a lot.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Conduction passes thermal energy through a material by particle vibration and, in metals, free electrons. Convection carries it in a moving fluid: warm fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises. Radiation carries it as infrared waves and needs no medium.
entries.simple: Heat moves three ways: through solids by conduction, in moving liquids and gases by convection, and through empty space by radiation.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A): current = charge / time. In metal wires the charge carriers are electrons. Conventional current is drawn from the positive terminal to the negative. In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere.
entries.simple: Current is how much electric charge flows past a point each second.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Potential difference, or voltage, is the energy transferred per unit of charge between two points, measured in volts (1 V = 1 J/C). A cell provides a voltage that pushes charge round the circuit; a voltmeter is connected in parallel to measure it.
entries.simple: Voltage is the push that drives current round a circuit.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Resistance measures how much a component opposes current, in ohms. Resistance = voltage / current. It is greater for a longer or thinner wire, and for most metals it rises with temperature.
entries.simple: Resistance is how hard a component makes it for current to flow.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Ohm's law: for a conductor at constant temperature, the current through it is directly proportional to the potential difference across it. So V = I x R, and a graph of current against voltage is a straight line through the origin. A filament lamp does not obey it because it heats up.
entries.simple: Ohm's law says that doubling the voltage across a resistor doubles the current through it.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: In a series circuit there is one path: the current is the same everywhere, the voltages across components add up to the supply voltage, and resistances add. In a parallel circuit each branch has the full supply voltage, the branch currents add up to the total, and the combined resistance is lower than the smallest branch.
entries.simple: In series, components share one loop and one current; in parallel, each has its own branch and its own share of the current.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: A wave transfers energy without transferring matter. In a transverse wave (light, water) the vibrations are at right angles to the direction of travel; in a longitudinal wave (sound) they are along it. Wave speed = frequency x wavelength. Frequency is the number of waves per second, in hertz.
entries.simple: A wave carries energy from place to place without carrying the material along with it.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Sound is a longitudinal wave of vibrations that needs a medium, so it cannot travel through a vacuum. It travels at about 340 m/s in air, faster in liquids and faster still in solids. Higher frequency means higher pitch; larger amplitude means louder.
entries.simple: Sound is vibrations travelling through air, water or solids to your ear.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave that travels at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum. Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum, which runs from radio waves through microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet and X-rays to gamma rays, in order of increasing frequency.
entries.simple: Light is a kind of wave that can travel through empty space, and it is the fastest thing there is.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: When light reflects from a smooth surface, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal. A plane mirror forms an upright virtual image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
entries.simple: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface, leaving at the same angle it arrived.

entries.subject: physics
aliases: why does a straw look bent
entries.text: Refraction is the change in direction of a wave when its speed changes on entering a different medium. Light bends towards the normal when it slows down (air to glass) and away when it speeds up. Snell's law: n1 sin i = n2 sin r. Beyond the critical angle, light inside the denser medium is totally internally reflected.
entries.simple: Refraction is light bending as it passes from one material into another, which is why a straw in water looks bent.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: A convex (converging) lens brings parallel rays to a focus at the principal focus; the distance from the lens to it is the focal length. A concave (diverging) lens spreads rays out. The lens formula links object distance, image distance and focal length.
entries.simple: A lens is a curved piece of glass that bends light to make things look bigger, smaller or sharper.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Sunlight is a mixture of all colours. Air molecules scatter short-wavelength blue light much more strongly than long-wavelength red light (Rayleigh scattering, proportional to 1/wavelength^4), so blue light reaches your eyes from every direction of the sky. At sunset the light crosses more air, most of the blue is scattered away, and the Sun looks red.
entries.simple: The air bounces blue light around far more than red light, so blue reaches your eyes from all over the sky.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: White light is a mixture of colours. Each colour is refracted by a slightly different amount in glass or water, so a prism or a raindrop spreads white light into a spectrum: red is bent least and violet most. A rainbow forms when sunlight is refracted, reflected and refracted again inside raindrops.
entries.simple: Raindrops split sunlight into its colours, the way a glass prism does.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: For small swings, the period of a simple pendulum depends only on its length and the strength of gravity, not on the mass of the bob or the size of the swing. Quadrupling the length doubles the period.
entries.simple: A longer pendulum swings more slowly; how heavy the bob is makes no difference.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: A projectile moves under gravity alone. Its horizontal velocity stays constant while its vertical velocity changes at 9.8 m/s2, so the path is a parabola. Ignoring air resistance, the range is greatest for a launch angle of 45 degrees.
entries.simple: A thrown ball keeps moving sideways at a steady speed while gravity pulls it down, so it follows a curved path.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Hooke's law: the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, up to the limit of proportionality. Force = spring constant x extension. Beyond the elastic limit the spring is permanently stretched.
entries.simple: Pull a spring twice as hard and it stretches twice as far, until you overstretch it.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: A magnet has a north and a south pole; like poles repel and unlike poles attract. The magnetic field around it is shown by field lines running from north to south. A current in a wire also produces a magnetic field, and coiling the wire round an iron core makes an electromagnet.
entries.simple: Magnets pull on iron and on each other: opposite ends attract and matching ends push apart.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: Rubbing two insulators together transfers electrons from one to the other. The one that gains electrons becomes negatively charged and the other positively charged. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
entries.simple: Static electricity is charge that builds up when things are rubbed together, like a balloon on your hair.

entries.subject: physics
entries.text: A scalar has size only: mass, time, distance, speed, energy, temperature. A vector has size and direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum. Vectors are added taking direction into account.
entries.simple: A scalar is just a number with a unit; a vector also has a direction.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: In algebra a variable is a letter that stands for a number. An expression combines numbers and variables, such as 3x + 2; an equation says two expressions are equal. The number multiplying a variable is its coefficient.
entries.simple: A variable is a letter standing in for a number you do not know yet.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: To solve a linear equation, do the same operation to both sides until the unknown is alone, undoing operations in reverse order. For 3x + 5 = 20: subtract 5 from both sides to get 3x = 15, then divide both sides by 3 to get x = 5. Check by substituting back.
entries.simple: Solving an equation is like keeping a balance level: whatever you do to one side, do to the other, until x is on its own.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: A straight line has the equation y = mx + c, where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept, the value of y where the line crosses the y-axis. Parallel lines have equal gradients; perpendicular lines have gradients that multiply to -1.
entries.simple: In y = mx + c, m tells you how steep the line is and c tells you where it crosses the y-axis.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: The gradient of a line is its steepness: the change in y divided by the change in x between any two points on it. A positive gradient slopes up from left to right, a negative one slopes down, and a horizontal line has gradient zero.
entries.simple: Gradient is how steep a line is: how far it goes up for each step across.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: A quadratic equation has the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 and its graph is a parabola. Solve it by factorising, completing the square or the quadratic formula. The discriminant b^2 - 4ac tells you the number of real roots: two if positive, one if zero, none if negative.
entries.simple: A quadratic is an equation with an x-squared in it; its graph is a U-shaped curve and it can have two answers.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input. f(x) = 2x + 1 means: double the input and add 1, so f(3) = 7. The set of allowed inputs is the domain and the set of possible outputs is the range.
entries.simple: A function is a number machine: put a number in and it gives exactly one number out.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse (the longest side, opposite the right angle) equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 is right-angled because 9 + 16 = 25.
entries.simple: In a right-angled triangle, square the two short sides and add them: you get the square of the longest side.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: In a right-angled triangle with angle x: sin x = opposite / hypotenuse, cos x = adjacent / hypotenuse and tan x = opposite / adjacent (SOH CAH TOA). The sine and cosine functions repeat every 360 degrees and always lie between -1 and 1.
entries.simple: Sin, cos and tan are ratios of the sides of a right-angled triangle that let you find missing sides and angles.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: A radian is the angle at the centre of a circle that cuts off an arc equal in length to the radius. A full turn is 2 pi radians, so 180 degrees = pi radians. Multiply degrees by pi/180 to convert to radians.
entries.simple: Radians are another way to measure angles: half a turn is pi radians instead of 180 degrees.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: The derivative of a function measures its instantaneous rate of change: the gradient of the tangent to its graph at a point. It is defined as the limit of the gradient of a chord as the two points close up. Power rule: the derivative of x^n is n x^(n-1), so the derivative of x^2 is 2x.
entries.simple: A derivative tells you how steep a curve is at one exact point, that is, how fast something is changing right then.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: A tangent is a straight line that just touches a curve at a point and has the same gradient as the curve there. The gradient of the tangent is the value of the derivative at that point.
entries.simple: A tangent is a straight line that just grazes a curve, showing which way the curve is heading at that spot.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: Integration is the reverse of differentiation and gives the area under a curve. To integrate x^n, raise the power by one and divide by the new power, then add a constant of integration: the integral of x^2 is x^3/3 + C.
entries.simple: Integration adds up lots of tiny pieces to find a total, such as the area under a curve.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: The limit of a function is the value it gets closer and closer to as the input approaches some value, even if the function is not defined exactly there. Limits are the foundation of both derivatives and integrals.
entries.simple: A limit is the value something heads towards as you get closer and closer, even if it never quite arrives.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: The mean is the total of the values divided by how many there are. The median is the middle value when they are in order. The mode is the most common value. The range, largest minus smallest, measures spread. The mean is pulled by extreme values; the median is not.
entries.simple: The mean is the fair share, the median is the middle one, and the mode is the most common one.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: Probability measures how likely an event is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). For equally likely outcomes it is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes. The probabilities of all possible outcomes add up to 1; for independent events, multiply the probabilities to find both happening.
entries.simple: Probability is a number between 0 and 1 that says how likely something is to happen.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: A ratio compares quantities, such as 2:3. Two quantities are directly proportional if doubling one doubles the other (y = kx, a straight line through the origin) and inversely proportional if doubling one halves the other (y = k/x).
entries.simple: A ratio compares how much of one thing there is to another; proportional things grow or shrink together.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: Per cent means out of 100. To find a percentage of an amount, multiply by the percentage divided by 100. Percentage change = (change / original) x 100.
entries.simple: A percentage is a fraction out of 100: 50% is a half.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: Standard form writes a number as A x 10^n, where A is at least 1 and less than 10 and n is a whole number. 3 x 10^8 means 300 000 000; 4.2 x 10^-3 means 0.0042. It keeps very large and very small numbers manageable.
entries.simple: Standard form is a short way to write very big or very small numbers using powers of ten.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: A logarithm is the power to which a base must be raised to give a number: log10(1000) = 3 because 10^3 = 1000. Logs turn multiplication into addition: log(ab) = log a + log b. The pH scale and the decibel scale are logarithmic.
entries.simple: A logarithm answers the question: what power of ten gives this number?

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount, the common difference d, each time; its nth term is a + (n - 1)d. A geometric sequence multiplies by the same ratio each time.
entries.simple: A sequence is a list of numbers that follows a rule, such as adding 3 each time.

entries.subject: maths
entries.text: Pi is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159. Circumference = 2 x pi x r and area = pi x r^2, where r is the radius. The diameter is twice the radius.
entries.simple: Pi, about 3.14, is how many times a circle's width fits round its edge.

entries.subject: lab
entries.text: The independent variable is the one you change on purpose. The dependent variable is the one you measure. Control variables are kept the same so that the test is fair and any change in the result is due to the independent variable alone.
entries.simple: In a fair test you change one thing, measure one thing and keep everything else the same.

entries.subject: lab
entries.text: An accurate result is close to the true value; precise results are close to each other. Random errors scatter readings and are reduced by repeating and averaging. Systematic errors shift every reading the same way, for example a balance that is not zeroed, and are not reduced by repeating.
entries.simple: Accurate means close to the right answer; precise means your repeats agree with each other.

entries.subject: lab
entries.text: A hypothesis is a testable explanation or prediction, usually written as: if I change this, then that will happen, because of this reason. An experiment collects evidence that supports or contradicts it; the conclusion says which.
entries.simple: A hypothesis is a sensible guess you can test with an experiment.

entries.subject: lab
entries.text: A liquid surface in a narrow tube curves; this curve is the meniscus. For water and most solutions, read the scale at the bottom of the meniscus with your eye level with it, to avoid parallax error.
entries.simple: Read the liquid level at the bottom of its curve, with your eye level with it.

entries.subject: lab
entries.text: Wear eye protection, tie back long hair and never taste or directly smell chemicals. Add acid to water, never water to acid. Point test tubes away from people when heating, know where the eyewash and fire blanket are, and tell a teacher at once about any spill or breakage.
entries.simple: Protect your eyes, never taste anything, and tell a teacher straight away if something spills or breaks.

entries.subject: lab
entries.text: The SI base units include the metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature) and mole (amount). Prefixes scale them: kilo = 1000, centi = 1/100, milli = 1/1000, micro = one millionth. Convert before calculating: 250 cm3 = 0.250 dm3.
entries.simple: Scientists everywhere use the same units, like metres, kilograms and seconds, so results can be compared.
